utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Kljajic. Do you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kljajic, could you make a solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljajic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Kljajic, if at any point of time you do not feel well, please do not hesitate to let us know. And there's one thing further that I'd like to advise you about, that is, the rule that we have at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljajic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Excellencies. Good day to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Kljajic. Good day, Mr. Ram.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, it's morning over there where you are. Mr. Kljajic, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can Mr. Ram show you a copy of that statement and can you tell us whether that's your statement?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read that statement?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you communicated to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Except for some minor details, I think that 99 per cent is the way I had put it to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for these details, do you feel it is necessary to indicate them and to correct them if they are of significance and if they change the meaning?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Basically, they're not very significant. It was mentioned here that I worked at the crime prevention service and I actually worked at the department that had to do with the tasks of the police, "milicija."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that? Could you please take a look.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 2. I think that it's line 6 or 7 where it says that I -- only to return to the post of inspector for crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is it supposed to read, inspector for affairs -- police affairs and tasks?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the rest of the statement faithfully reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today if I were to put the same questions to you, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: They would. The answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a copy from Mr. Ram and could you sign it before him and before us, and could you please put today's date there.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender Mr. Cedomir Kljajic's statement 1D7052, that is the number it bears now, and I would like to have it admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3917, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out a brief summary in the English language of Mr. Kljajic's statement. [In English] Cedomir Kljajic worked as police inspector in Sarajevo from 1987 to 1991. He was deputy to the assistant minister of police from September until October 1991 to the beginning of the war. When the war broke out, he was assigned to work in Vraca, where he occupied the post of under-secretary for public security. He remained in that position until August or September 1992. Cedo Kljajic was aware that the first party to be founded in BH was the SDA followed by the HDZ and finally SDS. During the SDA foundation assembly the Croatian and Muslim flags were tied together, showing the unity of the two ethnicities. These actions caused fear and concern amongst the Serbian people. Also during this period Cedo Kljajic was aware that the people were being armed and that more than 160.000 weapons entered B&H illegally. The overwhelming majority of the weapons were obtained by Muslims and Croats. Following the multi-party elections, a coalition was created between the SDA, SDS, and HDZ and the positions in the MUP were supposedly equally divided. On every level there were hypothetically one Muslim, one Serb, and one Croat. However, the SDA breached this agreement and people from the MUP were replaced by others who were not qualified. Cedo Kljajic discovered that he was not being consulted about changes of personnel in the MUP under his authority as he usually would be, and soon after he raised this issue he himself was replaced. New positions in the MUP were created and Serbian personnel were side-stepped. The Muslims were not only dominant in the top positions in the MUP but they also started to increase their numbers in lower positions. Also, the number of reserve policemen increased. These policemens were almost exclusively Muslims and only served the interests of the SDA. Mr. Cedomir Kljajic was aware that the Muslims were using the MUP to obtain equipment for the SDA. The security situation was getting worse by the day and as a result of all of this there was a need to divide up the BH MUP. The Serbs did not want a conflict. They knew it would result in massive bloodshed and therefore the Serbs embraced the Lisbon Agreement with enthusiasm and relief because they thought that a solution had been found to the problems. When the RS MUP was created, it had numerous problems including the lack of equipment, poor communication, lack of personnel, and the constant shelling of the base in Vrace. Further, some parts of the RS were physically completely inaccessible. In April 1991, Radovan Karadzic told Cedo Kljajic and the two others that the SDS had received certain positions in the MUP and that they could fill them; however, it was not necessary for them to be a member of the SDS. Karadzic asked that they work as the law requires, regardless of the violations of the law by their Muslim colleagues. Radovan Karadzic was adamant that the MUP must operate in accordance with the legal provisions and it was necessary to have a balance in the MUP between the staffs of the SDS and SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, perhaps I forgot to ask you something. In your statement perhaps instead of this Sime Djodan, should it have said Dalibor Brozovic, that is paragraph 3. Do you remember, was it Dalibor Brozovic or Sime Djodan?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I really cannot remember. I thought it was Sime Djodan. It's possible that it was Brozovic though. I know that his statement was very inflammatory. He said that the time came, that there had to be a border on the Drina, that this western bloc would exist again, and we Serbs in principle would not have any place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Excellencies, I don't have any further questions for Mr. Kljajic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How shall we understand paragraph 3 then?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood things correctly, Mr. Kljajic allows for the possibility that it wasn't Sime Djodan, that it was Dalibor Bozovic. He's not sure about the name but he knows it was a high-ranking Croat official who spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that. Mr. Kljajic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement, in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, it's not mentioned anywhere in your Defence statement, but you were interviewed at length by the Prosecution in 2003, and that statement was audio-recorded; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I understand from your statement that aside from one break of about five months between April and September of 1991, that you worked full time as a police official, first in the joint Bosnian MUP, then in the RS MUP for about 18 years, from 1974 until September 1992. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you a couple of questions about your position in the RS MUP. You stated that you were under-secretary for the public security service, and that's at paragraph 2 of your statement. And that meant essentially that you were in charge of the public security service of the RS MUP and you were accountable for its operation directly to the minister, Mico Stanisic; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the public security service was responsible for, among other things, threats to state security, the protection of citizens' lives and personal safety, the prevention and detection of criminal offences, tracking down and arresting perpetrators of criminal offences, and maintaining law and order. And that's from Article 15 of the RS Law on Internal Affairs P2964. Can you confirm that those items I listed were among the responsibilities of the public security service and indeed among your responsibilities as under-secretary?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: We had regulations for the interior and we were supposed to take care of preserving law and order and preventing crime and also detecting criminals.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So for what we understand as regular police work, preventing and detecting crime, arresting perpetrators, protecting citizens, you were the number three person in the ministry. The only people above you were the minister and his deputy; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at paragraph 4 of your statement you state that in the pre-war period you had information that people were being armed and that according to you the overwhelming majority of weapons were obtained by the Muslims, followed by the Croats, and the Serbs were third. Now, the RS MUP report for the period April to December 1992 describes activities of Serbian employees in the joint MUP before the war, activities which include "illegal arming of reliable active personnel and reserve employees." That's P2761, page 7. Now, before the war you were a high-level Serb employee in the MUP, so I take it that you were aware of this illegal arming among Serb police personnel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I think that you're wrong there. What I said, namely, that I knew that before the war about 160.000 fire-arms were illegal is a piece of information that I received from the representatives of the State Security Service. It was Brane Krstic's assistant, I think it was Zoranovic, I think that was his name. And at the end of 1990 we had some joint commission that went out there to the area of Mostar-Capljina because there were some conflicts between the army and the civilian population, and this was a Joint Commission of the Executive Council. In that commission there was a representative of the government, there was this representative of the State Security Service, and I was the third member of the commission. So there was a Muslim, there was a Croat, and a Serb. This representative of the State Security Service who was a Croat stated several times then that the State Security Service had reliable information to the effect that in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were over 160.000 long-barrelled weapons that were in Bosnia-Herzegovina illegally. By the way, by way of a joke sort of, he also pointed out: And these are Muslim weapons, these are the weapons of the Muslims. And by way of a joke, he also said: I'm not sure how much Croats have, but at any rate the Muslims managed to equip themselves well for a war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this more specific question. In September 1993, Tomo Kovac, who I assume you knew, reported that beginning in early 1991 he had been organising intense arming of citizens of Serbian nationality in Ilidza. That's P2308. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 15 of your statement you describe a July 1991 meeting of the SDS Deputies Club that you attended along with Mico Stanisic, Momcilo Mandic, and Vitomir Zepinic. And in your statement you say that Mico Stanisic praised you and Stanisic and Mandic criticised the work of Vito Zepinic. And you said that Dr. Karadzic reacted forcefully and criticised Zepinic. Now, I'd like to remind you of some additional things you told the OTP in 2003 about this meeting and ask you to confirm them. First you explained that this meeting and the criticism of Zepinic related to the fact that you had been recently demoted, you'd been demoted to the position of commander in charge of escorting trains, a position you rejected. And that's 65 ter 24950 at pages 23 and 24. Can you confirm that that's the context of your attendance at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know on which basis the meeting was called. I know that in the context Mico Stanisic said that we should come to that meeting. There were many people, many SDS members, but I hardly knew anyone except for Mr. Karadzic and that some other people I knew from TV. And some people demanded an explanation because they saw me and some other people. I believe that Slavko Draskovic was there and Kijac too. They saw people they didn't know and they were asking: Who are these people? What are they doing here? And then Mico Stanisic explained that we had come because there were some problems on the MUP, that there had been -- that I had been suddenly replaced, that the Muslims demoted me to a deputy commander after five or six years of being commander of that police station. It was part of their intention to humiliate me and return me to the same police station where I was, but only to the position of deputy commander. That's the lowest position for a person with a university degree. You probably know Sredoje Momic [as interpreted], who was transferred to the Novi Grad police station in Sarajevo. The plan was to humiliate people so that they refuse the position offered to them and as a consequence they'd be left without a job.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must intervene in the transcript. In line 14 we see "Sredoje Momic," which is wrong. It should be "Novic." And apart from that, the witness said that he was highly educated and experienced. He was in an executive position in the State Security Service, but he was transferred to a lower position which he refused. As for you, Mr. Kljajic, please speak slowly so that the interpreters don't have too difficult a job.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, do you confirm what Mr. Karadzic has said now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at this meeting, Mr. Kljajic, Dr. Karadzic not only criticised Zepinic, he slammed his hand on the table, yelled at Mr. Zepinic, and told him that if he did not get you re-instated, Zepinic would lose his job; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Probably my memory was fresher then. It's been ten years, after all. I don't remember all the details, but I believe that this is right. If I said it at the time, yeah, I think it was so. Mr. Karadzic must have been very angry with Mr. Zepinic because things were going on at the MUP and things were out of any control by the Serbs. People were replaced daily or removed daily --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: -- people were sent to police stations in the field --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, I'm going to interrupt you there because --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: -- for example --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but my question was quite specific and you were moving away from it. If we could -- if I could just show you what you said before quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 24950. It's page 25 in the English and page 33 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I believe the Registrar has a copy there he can show you. In and the English, it's about a third of the way down the page, it's roughly in the same position in the B/C/S where you described Dr. Karadzic slamming his hand against the table and yelling at Vito Zepinic: What are you doing? And then about two-thirds of the way down the page close to the bottom in the B/C/S you said: "And then Radovan Karadzic said, 'We all demand from you that you do this. You either do this or you'll lose your job.'" Does that remind you of what Dr. Karadzic -- how Dr. Karadzic reacted to Mr. Zepinic at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I think that during the meeting Dr. Karadzic really was angry at Mr. Zepinic and that he insisted that he take steps for the situation at the MUP to stabilise. However, objectively speaking from today's vantage point, Mr. Zepinic really couldn't do much because there was a combination of people at the MUP starting from Alija Delimustafic, Mr. Simovic, Avdo Hebib, Jusuf Pusina, the chief of communication and so on, Hajdar Hodzic who --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you again, but I am trying to ask very specific questions and I would ask you to try to keep your answers focused on those specific questions. Can you just confirm that you told the OTP in 2003 that Dr. Karadzic slammed his hand on the table at this meeting, yelled at Mr. Zepinic, and told him that if he did not get you re-instated that he would lose his job?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I think that Dr. Karadzic was angry and he probably slammed his hand on the table once. I don't think he -- I said he did it more than once. And I believe that he told Zepinic that he must re-instate me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 8 you talk about the division of the MUP. You said that there was a need to divide the MUP and you said that this was also what the Lisbon agreement provided for. Now, it's correct that whatever the Lisbon Agreement envisioned, it was never finalised. You acknowledged that in 2003 and that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: The truth is that the Lisbon Agreement envisaged a division, and more or less all of us at the ministry started behaving in accordance with it. Although, at some point Mr. Alija Izetbegovic changed his mind and gave up -- walked out from the Lisbon Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And the other thing about the Lisbon Agreement is that the evidence in this case indicates that the negotiations that culminated in this so-called agreement commenced on 13 February 1992. And that's D2968, paragraph 5. But senior Serb police personnel within the joint MUP, including yourself, were making concrete plans to divide the MUP even before this date. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: It wasn't only senior Serb personnel. Everybody did it. I can mention Alija Delimustafic and there was even mention of a division of buildings. The Muslims would get the building on Bozo Kovacevica Street, the Croats the one on Augusta Cerca [phoen] Street, and I think that two buildings were to go to the Serbs at the school of -- at the MUP school at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go to -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: And that was agreed at a collegium of the then-Minister of the Interior, Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P1083, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, these are minutes of a meeting held in Banja Luka on the 11th of February, 1992, and it indicates in the first paragraph your presence. Now, you did attend this meeting of Serb MUP personnel in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to point you to a few comments that are reflected in the minutes of this meeting, and the first is in the middle of page 1 in the English and near the bottom of the page in the B/C/S - and these are Mico Stanisic's remarks where he says: "Work has to be done by the organisation of the Serbian MUP, starting from the municipal and regional levels up to the Serbian ministry ..." And on the next page in the B/C/S and towards the bottom in the English, Nenad Radovic "notified those present that the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of BH had made a decision on the establishment of the Serbian MUP ..." And then you're the next speaker. And if we go to the next page in the English you state: "I categorically state that the SDA and the SDS cannot work in the same MUP. And if Nenad Radovic's proposal is not implemented within seven days, I will resign." The next speaker Andrija Bjelosevic, and this is on page 3 in the B/C/S, says at the end of his comments: "I also support the decision to establish the Serbian MUP." Goran Zugic, the next speaker, at the end of his comments, says: "The Serbian MUP has to start work as soon as possible ..." Predrag Jesuric, the next speaker, again at the end of his comments says: " ... the Serbian MUP should be established as soon as possible." Krsto Savic says: "We are already forming the Serbian Mostar SJB ..." Now, it's clear, Mr. Kljajic, that the main topic of this meeting or at least one of the topics was the creation of a separate Serb MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I think that the topic was the situation at the MUP. That was the main topic, and one of the other topics was the establishment of the Serbian MUP. And Nenad Radovic said that the Assembly of the Serbian people took that decision, and if it did we had no choice but to start working on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: It's another matter that the representatives of all the stations --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I would really prefer to let witness finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't follow the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I had started to speak and then I realised the witness was still speaking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue or should I --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- so I stopped --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll leave it to you. Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson. If necessary, the Chamber will intervene. Otherwise, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, if you would like to finish your answer, go ahead, please, briefly.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I think you interrupted me when I was about to say that at that meeting the situation was analysed and all representatives of public security stations and security services centres exerted great pressure on us and criticised us for not doing anything at the ministry. That we were being inactive and irresponsible on that, we didn't deserve to be in our positions, that we should leave those positions and make room for new people to do the job as it should be done. And I pointed out at the meeting that if in the coming 10 or 15 days we really showed that we weren't determined enough to do anything, that I will resign so that somebody else may be able to do the job better than I. And after some time I did that. I handed in my resignation and retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, if you could concentrate on answering the question. The question put to you this time was whether the topic at the time was a creation of a separate Serbian MUP. What is your answer to that, Mr. Kljajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is affirmative. I believe Nenad Radovic phrased it best. He informed us that the Assembly of the Serbian People had taken that decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljajic, when you were shown this document in 2003, you agreed that the officials present at this meeting were not implementing something that had been agreed with the Muslims. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember what you're asking me about now. I don't remember that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, if we could then -- I'll just remind you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page -- to 65 ter 24950, again. This is page 52 of the English and page 70 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the bottom of page 52 in the English and towards the bottom of page 70 in the B/C/S, you're asked: "Mr. Kljajic, is there any reference," and then there's something unintelligible, "agreement with Muslims in respect of division of MUP?" And this is in the context of your discussion of this document, and you say at the top of the next page in English: "No, there is no reference in this document ... this is something that was mentioned and discussed every day." And then in the next page in the B/C/S and skipping down two paragraphs in the English, SM asks you at the end of his question: "Are you saying that all of these officials who got together were doing something that was agreed with the Muslims?" And you answer: "No." And you're asked again: "So, the proposal set out in this document was not agreed with the Muslims?" And you say: "No." Now, that's what you said in 2003, right, that the proposals at this 11 February 1992 meeting were not proposals that had been agreed to with the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, if you're asking me whether we had written down these proposals and given it to the Muslims to work on them, my answer is no. But whether there was previous discussion at the collegium of the minister of the MUP, then the answer is yes. In other words, were these proposals put on paper before we discussed them? No, they weren't. But at any rate, there was discussion about this matter at many collegium meetings at the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender these two pages of the interview, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive the first page and these two pages. Shall we assign a number for this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6468, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljajic, I'd like to ask you now about the barricades in Sarajevo in early March, which you discussed in 2003, and I will ask you to please, if you -- I'm going to put a series of short propositions to you, and if you could please just affirm that it's correct if you agree that it's correct, and if there's anything that you need to add at the end, you can do so. So in 2003 you explained that when the blockade of Sarajevo started with barricades put up by the Serbs, you were called to go urgently to the MUP headquarters. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you arrived, Momcilo Mandic, then chief of public security, took you on a tour of the barricades and introduced you to the people manning the barricades and told you all of their names; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer merely yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like you to please answer yes or no if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I think I owe you an explanation - although you're insisting that I do so at the end, because I may forget until then. When I came to the MUP, everybody was there, not only Serbs. And this should not be considered to have been that way. Everybody was there, Serbs, Muslims, Croats. At one point we had a meeting for us to be informed of the situation on the ground, and Momcilo Mandic asked me to accompany him, to go to the Holiday Inn. And on our way there we saw those roadblocks and we saw some people at the check-points that he knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In 2003 you said: "He invited me to come with him and tour these barricades. We toured the barricades at Vrbanja bridge and Pofalici. I have omitted to mention that when we were touring the barricades he introduced me to the people who were manning these barricades." That's what you said in 2003. Can you confirm that that's correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I think that it's a fact that he told me we were going to the Holiday Inn, and on the way there we also called up those barricades if we want to be fully precise and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to tender what I just read out which is page 20 of the English and page 27 and 28 of the B/C/S and add that to P6468, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, since it's been read out in its entirety, Mr. President, I don't know that that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think if the witness doesn't accept his prior statement, then the prior statement itself should be admitted as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Better to have them in written evidence. We'll add them to the exhibit. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kljajic, you mentioned that Mr. Mandic was taking you to the Holiday Inn, and he indeed took you to the SDS headquarters at the Holiday Inn where you met with a number of people including Rajko Dukic and Nedjo Vlaski who was then a DB official. That's page 21 of the English. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not meet with him. It was not a meeting. They were doing their job. We came to their office. We simply arrived there, we sat down, and they continued doing what they had been doing before. It was not a formal meeting. It was not like we had arrived in order to attend a meeting that was scheduled before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what Rajko Dukic was busy doing at the time was talking on two or three telephone lines, and it became clear to you that he was handling everything and was the main organiser. That's page 22. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I realised that he was the one who was in charge of that activity within the SDS, that he was the most responsible person, the number one person.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you observed that Rajko Dukic was informing Radovan Karadzic, who was abroad at the time, on the latest developments regarding the barricades; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I believe that he did talk with Mr. Karadzic on the phone and that he put him in the picture, he told him about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you some more questions about Mr. Mandic. In 2003 when you were asked about the period before the war, you compared Mr. Mandic and Mr. Zepinic as follows. You described Mr. Mandic as aggressive and unscrupulous, whereas Zepinic was composed, calm, and decent. That's page 19. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: That was how I saw things. It was my free estimate of the things, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you said that Mandic was very influential and acted as if he were the deputy minister instead of Zepinic. That's page 19. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: That was in keeping with his personality. He liked to behave in that way. I believe that in some cases he appeared to be more important than Mr. Zepinic, that he was the deputy minister and not Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in light of this behaviour of Mr. Mandic, you assessed that he must have had the support of Dr. Karadzic. That's page 20. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: At that time, that seemed to be logical, that he enjoyed more support from Mr. Karadzic and the SDS, which is why he behaved in the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after the war began you told the OTP in 2003 that you arrived at the Vrace school the day after it had been taken over by the special forces, and that from the moment you arrived it was clear to you that Mandic was bent on illegal activities. That's page 33. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in particular, you observed that Mandic, with his associates, was taking away everything that he pleased from the Vrace school with a 2-tonne freight vehicle, including valuable property, passports, and car registration papers. That's pages 33 to 34. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And on one occasion Branko Djeric, the prime minister, told you that Mandic had made a gift of nine Golf vehicles to the RS government, but you knew these vehicles were stolen from the Sarajevo airport and you told Mr. Djeric that; right? That's page 37.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Djeric was taken aback by what you told him and after that it appeared to you that Mr. Djeric wanted to replace Mandic but was not powerful enough; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric was taken aback. As a matter of fact, that was my interpretation which was based on the information that I had collected. In the meantime I've read some books and some newspaper articles, and I realised that Mr. Djeric did have an intention to remove Mr. Mandic from his position but he failed in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you complained to Mico Stanisic about Mandic's activities, and Stanisic told you he couldn't do anything about it because Krajisnik had said Mandic was the best minister in the government. That's page 32 and 33. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you told the OTP that Mandic and Stanisic were very close, they were connected by the kum relationship, and you believed that that relationship continued throughout 1992, in part because you and others complained to Mr. Stanisic about Mandic's criminality but Stanisic never did anything about it. Pages 35 and 36. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Stanisic did, whether he tried to do something. I suppose that I concluded that based on the information that I'd had up to then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 11 of your statement you said that you spent roughly the first month and a half of the war in Vrace, and then you were about 15 days in Pale before you transferred to Bijeljina. So I take it you were in Vrace from roughly early April until roughly mid-May 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you told the OTP in 2003 that during the time you were in Vrace you went to Belgrade for ten days to visit your family. That's page 34. Can you confirm that; and if so, did you travel back and forth to Belgrade by car?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I went to Belgrade, but I travelled by helicopter there and back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, line 16 in your question, you referred to kum relationship between Mandic and Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I can ask a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the kum relationship that Mandic and Stanisic had entailed? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: The kum relationship is a form of a friendly relationship. It is not a family relationship. However, a kum is somebody's best man at his wedding. That would be the kum relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now you just mentioned travelling to Belgrade by helicopter, and again in 2003 you were played an intercept, which is in evidence as P2227, from the 18th of April, where you were speaking with Mr. Mihajlovic, and in that intercept you said that helicopters were flying every day back and forth from the Pale or Vrace area to Belgrade. Can you confirm that helicopters were going back and forth on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that. I doubt that I ever said that they travelled every day, but they did travel from Pale to Belgrade, not from Vrace to Belgrade. And the main purpose of those flights were to transport the wounded. And whenever the wounded were transported, there would be a place left unoccupied. So we made the most of the opportunity and we travelled on those helicopters to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have P2227, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to remind you of what you said in that conversation. As you can see this is an intercept of conversation between you and Pero Mihajlovic on the 18th of April. And if we can go to page 2 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S. And it's towards the bottom of the page in both languages, and you're discussing with Mr. Mihajlovic whether he will come to see you and you say: "There are helicopters flying between Belgrade and here daily." And Mihajlovic says: "I can't reach him, damn it," talking about Mico Davidovic. And you say: "You should ask around. They are operating constantly." Does that remind you of what you said on the 18th of April, 1992, about helicopters operating -- flying between Belgrade and Pale daily or constantly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, there was just one or perhaps two helicopters that transported the wounded from Pale to the military medical academy in Belgrade, and this is what the conversation is about. I urged him to get on one of those helicopters and return to Pale together with the wounded. That's what I was telling him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Again, at paragraph 12 of your statement you discuss communication problems in the MUP at the beginning of the war. Now, in 2003 it was put to you that by the 20th of April, 1992, the ministry was producing daily bulletins on security-related events based on information received regularly from the CSBs. And you claim that you were not aware that there was communication between the CSBs and the ministry and that you had never seen these daily bulletins. And that's pages 69 and 72. Is that still your claim, Mr. Kljajic, that although you were the number three person in the ministry, you didn't know that there was communication between the CSBs and the ministry or that the ministry produced daily bulletins based on that information?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that you have to understand my position and my role at the time. I was in Vrace and the Ministry of the Interior was in Pale. The communication between the centres and the ministry at Pale bypassed me. I simply did not have any insight into the type of communication that they may have had, what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 15 the witness said that he was seconded to Vrace. This is missing from the transcript. Vrace was not close to Pale and this is missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljajic, despite your claims that you don't know about communication between the CSBs and the ministry, it's correct that you directly received a report from the Bijeljina CSB in mid-April when you were in Vrace by telephone. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to D1694, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljajic, you can see on page 1 that you introduced yourself. About six lines down, you say: "This is Cedo Kljajic speaking." And the respondent says: "Cedo, this is Jesuric, chief from Bijeljina speaking." That would be Predrag Jesuric, CSB chief in Bijeljina; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember now receiving a report on the 16th of April from Mr. Jesuric reporting on the situation in the Bijeljina CSB area?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: This is not a report. Do you know what a report should look like? When you look at this conversation and when you put it on paper, it will fit on one single page. Reports are more extensive. They go over four, five, or six pages. This is just an overview, a short conversation that you are now trying to portray as a report. This is a simple conversation between myself and Jesuric.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look a little more at this simple conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Gustafson, shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 25 minutes, but before doing so we'll -- there's one thing I'd like to discuss in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 25 minutes and resume at seven past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, I was asking you some questions about this conversation between you and Mr. Jesuric on the 16th of April, 1992. And at the top of the page in both languages, Mr. Jesuric reports that everything is normal in Bijeljina and the situation in Zvornik is getting back to normal. You say: "All right." And he says: "15.000 Muslims escaped to Serbia which means that they are not afraid of Serbs and that they have trust from Serbia to Serbia." And you ask: "Escaped to Mali Zvornik, is that right?" And Jesuric says: "Yes." And you say: "To Serbia. Escaped to Serbia. All right." Now, you would agree that a report that 15.000 Muslims have escaped Zvornik. That's a pretty alarming piece of information; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say this. He shared that with us as a piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you as under-secretary for public security responsible for protecting lives and safety of citizens, maintaining law and order, and detecting possible criminal offences, you didn't find this piece of information, that 15.000 Muslims had escaped Zvornik, to cause you any concern?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Look, objectively speaking I believe that this is blown out of proportion, this figure of 15.000 people who fled at one moment. There may have been a couple thousand who fled, and you know that operations were going on there. There was war going on. And it is only normal that under such circumstances people leave, that they flee the war. I don't see anything out of the ordinary here if people decided to cross the river to go to Serbia to save themselves from the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say they decided. It says they escaped. And you said: "It is only normal that under such circumstances," referring to operations, "people leave." But, Mr. Kljajic, you didn't ask Mr. Jesuric what caused these people to leave. You didn't -- you didn't know whether they were leaving due to combat, whether they were being forced out, what had happened to these people, why 15.000 people of only one ethnicity had left the municipality in a short period of time. You didn't ask any of those questions, did you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I did not ask any of those questions because at the time you could hear on the radio and watch on TV that there was combat going on there. It was a logical conclusion that that was the reason. I believe that a certain number of Serbs also escaped; however, that moment he didn't speak about Serbs who had fled the combat area. It is only normal to people to flee from an area of combat operations. I don't know what you think I could do as an under-secretary who was in Vrace to save those people, to provide them with safety in an area of combat operations. Do you really think that one person could do something, especially in view of the fact that I didn't have power in my hands? I was an individual who worked in Vrace. I didn't have a single man under my control or my command. So are you saying that I should have gone there as an individual and that I should have stopped those people? That I should have them: People, stop, you have to stay?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So let me get this straight, Mr. Kljajic: As someone with 18 years service as a professional police official who was the under-secretary for public security, you get a report from the CSB chief in Bijeljina that 15.000 Muslims have left Zvornik and your professional decision is to assume that they're fleeing due to combat and you see no need as a professional to ask Mr. Jesuric any follow-up questions about these people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Look, read the report through and you will see that at the end Jesuric tells me that he will send the report to Pale. Whatever the two of us discussed, he would forward to the Ministry of the Interior. And that was just a piece of extra information. And what do you think that I should have done at that moment? I would love you to tell me what I was supposed to do as a professional. The only thing I could do was to acknowledge that. I didn't have any effective power, any possibility to prevent war operations. I could only acknowledge that information as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned that there were operations in Zvornik at this time, and you knew that Arkan was involved, didn't you? You told the OTP in 2003 that it was well-known that Arkan had operations in Bijeljina, Brcko, and Zvornik; and after that, he carried out extensive looting and took as much as he could for himself. That's page 137. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I received that kind of information. I was not there. I received that information from other people and I interpreted it in the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 16 of your statement you describe a meeting you attended in Belgrade in May of 1992 about a month after the conflict began, attended by the chiefs of CSBs, RS MUP officials, and Dr. Karadzic. Now, in 2003 you told the OTP that you thought Mr. Krajisnik was there as well, that's page 68. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that meeting. I said that I thought that meeting had taken place and that he had been there, but I can't remember that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I assume that Mr. Stanisic, the minister, was there as well, Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you said in your statement, Defence statement, that Dr. Karadzic informed those present about the general situation and issues. I take it from that that Dr. Karadzic was better informed than the MUP leadership about the situation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, he spoke in general terms, and what he told us is everything that we could see on TV. That information was publicly available. He told us that war operations had started, that there were dead and wounded, that we had to take that into account, and he told us that on our side we had to remain as professional as possible, that we had to implement laws and regulations that applied to the work of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said he told you that there were dead and wounded. Did he tell you any more details than that about who was dead and wounded? Did he tell you who, where, or when?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember that he shared any detail with us. He told us that we should comply with the Geneva Conventions, the Law on War, and that the Ministry of the Interior had to act within the framework of the Law on the Interior and our rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did Dr. Karadzic ask Mr. Stanisic or any of the other police officials there for any specific information or reports or ask for any information to be gathered and reported back to him?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that he asked anyone for anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 10 of your statement you said that you never heard from any of your colleagues in the MUP or other members of the civilian and military authorities that Muslims or Croats should be expelled. But you did know at the time that, in the summer of 1992 in particular, that the Republika Srpska authorities were capturing large numbers of Muslims and detaining them in terrible conditions in makeshift camps guarded by MUP officials. You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Never really did anyone speak about that kind of thing in front of me; I can assert that. No officials within the Ministry of the Interior or political representatives or military representatives, no one ever spoke of any kind of expulsion of Muslims or Croats. As for these camps, I just knew of this one camp, I think it was at Manjaca, the one that Mr. Zupljanin spoke about and he said the conditions were rather bad there and that something would have to be done. So roughly the conclusion was that the best solution was to carry out an exchange of prisoners, Serb and Croat prisoners, all for all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When did Mr. Zupljanin tell you that the conditions in Manjaca were rather bad?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, he just said that there was this camp there that had been established and the conditions were not exactly adequate and that actually this is a burden for the MUP, that he wanted that to be resolved as soon as possible, and that was the conclusion, that this should be resolved by having exchange all for all. So that the Muslims would release all of our prisoners and we would release all of their prisoners, and that would be the only right and rapid solution. They were a problem for us. What to do with these people? There was always the possibility of some abuse on the part of individuals who could have abused these people in some way. So it was really in no one's interests.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I have D477, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Mr. Kljajic, my question was when Mr. Zupljanin told you about poor conditions in Manjaca. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I think that at this meeting he said a few sentences, that the conditions were not good and that this question should be resolved urgently by way of an exchange, all for all. All the prisoners held by the Serbs for all the prisoners held by the Muslims and that that would be the only solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm -- I think I misspoke. I think it should be D447. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But this is nice document, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljajic, this is a summary of a meeting of senior MUP officials from the 11th of July, 1992. And if we go to page 2 you can see that it indicates that you, among others, are present. Now, you attended this meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 7 of the English and page 8 in the B/C/S in e-court, and it's actually page 5 in the original numbering of the document in B/C/S for the Registrar's benefit. And it's the second paragraph in B/C/S and it's in the middle in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Zupljanin is speaking and he says: "The army and Crisis Staffs or War Presidencies are requesting that as many Muslims as possible are gathered and they are leaving these undefined camps up to the internal affairs organs. Conditions in these camps are bad. There is no food. Some individuals do not observe international norms ...," et cetera. And do you remember Mr. Zupljanin describing multiple camps in which as many Muslims as possible were being gathered and detained and these camps were left to be secured by MUP officials?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Zupljanin said that in the context of our obligations on the basis of the law and that it was in that context that this discussion took place at that meeting and it was stated that organs of the interior cannot in any way be the ones in charge of camps that were set up by the military. If the military set them up, then they should provide security there too. From the point of view of the Law on the Interior, and that was one of the conclusions, it was unacceptable for us to deal with improvised camps. Because if we are to give our people there to secure these camps, then we would not have enough people for preserving public law and order in the territory that is under the control of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that was Mr. Zupljanin's concern, right, that there were too many -- that the police were too busy securing these improvised collection facilities to be -- and they weren't able to carry out their regular police duties; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zupljanin made these comments orally. I think that this report or whatever it was that he wrote, he contributed that to the transcript or the minutes and we did not hear all of it perhaps. Truth to tell, he did say there that he thought that that was not the best way, how the organs of the interior should be involved, and he expressed his fear that some members of the police may overstep their authority, abuse these people who are in the camp. And he was afraid of that. He said that he thought that we had to resolve the matter, namely, that the army should take over these camps again and that we should deal with our own work.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And earlier you mentioned that Mr. Zupljanin had discussed Manjaca, but it's clear this isn't just about Manjaca, right, he refers to undefined camps being left up to the internal affairs organs and that these collection centres, plural, are not adequate. This isn't just about Manjaca. This is a widespread phenomenon; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said to you that Mr. Zupljanin provided this information in writing too. Here he spoke - it was an oral statement and it was about Manjaca. Now, 21 years ago whether he mentioned some other camps, I cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, you have expressed quite some recollections about this meeting and these comments in particular by Mr. Zupljanin. Do you remember that in 2003, ten years ago, when you were asked about these comments you said that you didn't remember whether these camps existed or if they were discussed as a problem at this meeting? Do you remember that ten years ago you basically said you had no recollection of these comments?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: It is possible that I said it at that moment. I don't know why I said that. In the meantime I got quite a bit of information through the media, on the internet, read different books. It is possible that in that context, I mean now, I am putting this together, things that I did not remember at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just go quickly to 65 ter 24950 at page 160 in the English and, in fact, there's no B/C/S transcript for this portion of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Registrar in Canada, the page numbers are in the upper right-hand corner, the consecutive page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, do you understand English and read English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljajic, you've said you don't understand English so I'll read the relevant passages to you where you're being asked about this document we just looked at and this comment from Mr. Zupljanin in particular. And you're -- it says -- you're asked: "This meeting took place on the 11th of July 1992. Can you confirm that as ... July 1992 you had knowledge of these camps?" And you say: " ... you have to believe me, I really don't remember. I can't recollect any of these things, it's a long paragraph, you see, I don't remember any of these details." And you're asked: "Do you recall what the Crisis Staffs and the Army ...," and then there's something inaudible, "persons and left them in camps?" And you say: "I cannot remember that, because I was not there, in the field, I was specifically at Vraca and these activities took part on the ground, somewhere in the area of Banja Luka." And you're asked: "Can you confirm that these camps were left under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Internal Affairs?" And you say: "I can see that from these minutes, from what I said here in the minutes, but I really don't remember that these camps existed and that we discussed them as some sort of problem." You're asked: "Do you remember that the conditions in the camps were poor?" And you say: "I never toured a single camp and I can't confirm that the conditions were either bad or good." And you're asked: "Did you consider that the involvement of the police in the management of these camps was a serious issue?" And you answer: "I don't remember that." So, Mr. Kljajic, you can that -- can you confirm that in 2003, ten years ago, you stated that you basically had no recollection of these comments at this meeting, in contrast to what you've testified to today?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm telling you, in order to clarify this thing that you wish to know about, in the meantime I received a lot of information. I looked at a lot of clips on YouTube, I read different books, articles, and probably in the meantime my knowledge about all of that was completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you've given evidence about what Mr. Zupljanin said at this meeting and what he meant at this meeting. So is it your testimony that your evidence about what Mr. Zupljanin said and meant at this meeting is influenced by what you've seen on YouTube or read in books and articles?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, look, Mr. Zupljanin at that moment - as I've already said - attached his report and I never had an opportunity of seeing it before it was presented to me in The Hague. I never saw it. We were at that meeting. Mr. Zupljanin spoke briefly and I really do not recall. I really cannot recall all the details of everything he said then. Obviously in that report he wrote about that, as is stated here in this document of yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, my time I think is up in the next five minutes. I need to deal with two brief topics, so I would ask, if I could, for an extra 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, I'd like to ask you to confirm some information you gave to the OTP about Predrag Jesuric, the Bijeljina CSB chief, that you gained from your time when you were based in Bijeljina. You told the OTP that one of the paramilitary units in Bijeljina, Mauzer's Panthers were essentially operating under Predrag Jesuric. You said that Jesuric was the brains and Mauzer was the executive power behind him. That's page 82. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: That is the information that I had. That's true that I stated that. That's the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And at one point due to complaints about Jesuric's work, you spoke to Mico Stanisic to try to get Jesuric transferred out of Bijeljina. That's page 138. That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked Mico Stanisic several times to get Jesuric out of Bijeljina because I thought that he was this factor of disruption in Bijeljina, that he disrupted relations in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you later learned that Jesuric had spoken to Mico Stanisic and had convinced Stanisic to allow Jesuric to remain in Bijeljina and part of that convincing exercise was Jesuric promising to give Stanisic an Audi and a BMW; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: That is the same information that I learned of indirectly, through my co-workers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then you spoke to Mico Stanisic and he told you that he'd spoken to Jesuric and that Jesuric could stay in Bijeljina, and Stanisic asked you to bring him the two cars that Jesuric had promised him, a request that you refused to carry out. That's page 139. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, if I stated that then it is certainly correct. Now I no longer remember that, it's been another ten years since then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 139 of the English and page 153 of the B/C/S of your interview. And this is at the top of the page in English and in the middle of the B/C/S, and here you explain that Mr. Pantic, who was the SJB chief, told you that Jesuric had told him that he -- Jesuric had convinced Stanisic that he could remain in Bijeljina and promised to give him the two cars. And then you say that you had a conversation with Mico Stanisic and he told you that he'd talked to Jesuric and that there was no need for Jesuric to go to the MUP headquarters, that everything would be okay in Bijeljina. And you say: " ... and then he asked me to bring to the ministries two cars that were then in Bijeljina and to transport them to the ministry and to give him, the ministry, the keys for the cars which I naturally never carried out." Does that remind you of your conversation with Mr. Stanisic when he asked you to bring him the two cars that Jesuric had promised?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Well, this has not reminded me, absolutely not, but I believe that what was stated then is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I have one last document I'd like to show you and it's not -- there's no hard copy there in Canada, so I'm going to ask the usher to please put it on the ELMO so that you can see it across the videolink --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's possible because ELMO is being used for the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I spoke to the AV people before court and they told me that it would be so. We can try it out and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll sort it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will check it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that it would be possible but we could not see the witness. Let's proceed. Mr. Kljajic, can you confirm that you can see the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender the document I had on the ELMO, although it needs some parts of it to be translated from the B/C/S. So if it could be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it and mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6469 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. Only a couple of questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljajic, you mentioned that you stated something because at that time you had such information. Was such information checked and were -- was it proved true or was it part of a blackening campaign --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, I have no idea what Dr. Karadzic is referring to here. You stated something because at that time you had such information, I think the question needs to be more specific. I can't follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he mentioned he checked something, but could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll go question by question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the exact position or job title of Mr. Jesuric?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jesuric was chief of the Bijeljina SUP at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see D1436.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he in that position long -- oh, you cannot see this. But then I'll read it out to you. It's a report about an audit or as it says here an inspection conducted on situation found at SJB Bijeljina. And on page 4 -- actually, page 5 it says: "Their demands according to our information have to do with the removal -- unconditional removal of chief Predrag Jesuric ..." and so on. Was he chief of the crime enforcement service at any time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: When I and Mico Stanisic came to Bijeljina, he was chief of crime enforcement, whereas Aco - I can't remember his last name - was the SUP chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is the name Pantic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the name, Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2881, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out because you cannot see it -- or can you? Do you have it there?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I have a report here. I don't know if this is it. It's dated 26 June to 25 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. I'll read out the second part of the sentence in paragraph 1. "Certain personnel changes occurred in the department for -- of prevention and detection of crimes ..." And then we'll go to the next page, the third paragraph from the bottom, which mentions Arkan's men. It says here: "89 pistols and three hunting rifles were illegally registered with the Bijeljina SJB with the knowledge of the then-Chief Predrag Jesuric and the general affairs department head ..." Based on all this, was he removed?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason for that rotation was. I know that Predrag Jesuric was SUP chief before the war and when Mico Stanisic and I went there, it may have been in May or early June, he was chief of crime enforcement, whereas Aco Pantic, whom he appointed as SUP chief, was SUP chief. There was this rotation, but if he was removed because of that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today on page 42 of the transcript which you probably cannot see, you mentioned that there were demands for Jesuric to be removed. Was this case involving Jesuric an exception or not and what was the attitude of the MUP toward shortcomings in the work of their own officials?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: I believe that the RS MUP made efforts to function in accordance with the law and the regulations. Whoever did not was basically exposed to disciplinary sanctions, just as in peace time. We didn't replace people ad hoc as if there was a war on. We tried to follow the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position of the organs, that is, the Serbian authorities, before the war and the authorities of the RS when the war started and it began functioning? Did you receive support from them or were you obstructed?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: No one obstructed us on that. On the contrary, we always enjoyed support. In all contacts with you, you always insisted that we work in accordance with the law and the regulations, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 32 of today's transcript you were asked what you as chief of public security whose task it is to preserve law and order, what you did in areas of combat activity, what were you able to do there?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't the question. I mean, that was a total mis-characterisation of what I had said. If he wants to ask the question, I don't have an objection, but without the mis-characterisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you rephrase your question, Mr. Karadzic, based upon the actual transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about the number of Muslims who were crossing to Serbia from municipalities along the border. What were you able to do? Did those people go to Serbia because of disruptions in public law and order or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, that's a totally leading way of asking the question. Just ask it in an open-ended way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the reason why those people went there and what did your service -- what means of intervention did your service have at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR KLJAJIC
utterances.text: First of all, we must know that at that time communication between us and SJBs out there were very bad, barely existing. All we could do was send Telex messages but the enemy was able to listen in. Whatever we sent out by Telex or received by Telex was also read by the enemy. The same applies to phone lines, and you can see that from intercepts. Everything was eavesdropped. So we could send the information to Sarajevo and Sarajevo could forward that information to them at the same time. There was no direct, dedicated phone line between us and the public security stations. And we were unable to issue any orders to those public security stations, either directly or indirectly, except by sending messages by courier. And of course that took quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see D4447 [as interpreted] again, page 20 and it's 18 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the page where that starts with the name "Planojevic" or the section that starts with his name. We got the right document although the number is wrong in the transcript.
